questions.answer: The classifier transforms the current formant evidence using its existing parameters. A physical filter change alters the evidence it receives, while learning would involve changing the network weights.
rubric: Trace a changed physical feature pair into the network’s computation.
Separate changed input evidence from changed learned parameters.
questions.topic: From a physical change to classifier evidence

questions.prompt: The membrane animation has equally spaced labeled frequencies and equal pickup peaks. Explain what was chosen for this teaching example and what broader physical claim it does not establish.
questions.answer: The frequencies were assigned as illustrative harmonics, and the modal coefficients were chosen to give equal peaks at the specified pickup. The example demonstrates combining spatial modes and reading their components. Those choices do not establish that the rectangular membrane’s natural frequencies are equally spaced or that another measurement point would show the same amplitudes.
rubric: Identify the assigned illustrative frequency spacing.
Identify the pickup-dependent amplitude construction.
Keep the demonstrated combination of modes separate from a universal natural-frequency claim.
questions.topic: What a schematic membrane spectrum establishes

questions.prompt: Explain how a stationary fixed endpoint and a maximally moving free endpoint constrain the shape of an allowed mode before you read any numerical frequency label.
questions.answer: The shape must have a displacement node at the fixed end and a displacement antinode at the free end. Starting at the node, an odd number of quarter-wave packets reaches the antinode. The resulting shapes have different numbers of internal reversals while preserving the two end conditions. This is why the illustrated sequence selects odd rather than consecutive integer multiples.
rubric: Use the fixed node and free antinode as simultaneous constraints.
Explain the odd quarter-wave fit in terms of those constraints.
Connect higher allowed shapes with additional spatial reversals.

questions.prompt: How would you use the air-element animation to distinguish back-and-forth particle motion from compression if a still frame made their difference unclear?
questions.answer: I would track the same marked region over several phases. The movement of individual elements relative to their resting positions reveals displacement. The changing separation of neighboring elements reveals compression and rarefaction. Comparing both across time prevents a crowded-looking frame from being mistaken for the region of largest particle excursion.
rubric: Track particle excursion through time.
Separately track changes in neighbor spacing.
Use the two observations to distinguish motion from compression.
questions.topic: Following air through a vibration cycle

questions.prompt: Why is “the constriction increases both mass and stiffness” insufficient by itself to predict the sign of a particular formant shift?
questions.answer: The two changes matter according to different local properties of the mode. Added effective mass matters where the air moves strongly, while increased stiffness matters where compression or stretching is strong. A constriction’s location must therefore be compared with the specified mode’s pattern before deciding which effect dominates. Equal mention of two properties does not imply equal influence.
rubric: Relate the mass effect to local motion.
Relate the stiffness effect to local deformation.
Explain why location and mode identity are required before predicting direction.
questions.topic: Why a constriction needs a local analysis

questions.prompt: The illustrated /u/ and /i/ models both lower F1 but differ in their F2 shifts. Explain how the first-mode agreement can coexist with the second-mode difference.
questions.answer: The /u/ lip loading is motion-dominated for both first modes, so added effective mass lowers both frequencies. At the /i/ region, the first-mode mass effect still lowers F1, but strong local deformation gives the second-mode stiffness effect greater influence and raises F2. Agreement in one resonance does not imply that the two constrictions occupy equivalent positions in another mode.
rubric: Explain mass dominance for the two /u/ modes.
Explain the different second-mode dominance at the /i/ region.
Connect the comparison to mode-specific local patterns.
questions.topic: A shared first-mode shift with different second-mode shifts

questions.prompt: A classmate says the /a/ example raises F1 because mass has begun to increase frequency. Give the spatial explanation that corrects that account.
questions.answer: The /a/ location places the first mode in a region where compression and springiness dominate, so increased stiffness raises F1. The second mode is more motion-dominated there, so the mass effect lowers F2. The mass rule has not reversed; moving the constriction changes which local contribution dominates each resonance.
rubric: Assign the upward F1 shift to stiffness dominance.
Assign the downward F2 shift to mass dominance.
Keep the physical directions unchanged while explaining the changed spatial weighting.
questions.topic: The /a/ reversal as a spatial explanation

questions.prompt: Why should a description such as “a constriction one-third of the way along the tract” state whether the distance is measured from the glottis or from the lips?
questions.answer: The two ends define different reference directions along the tract. A location described as two-thirds from the glottis can also be one-third back from the lips, whereas one-third from the glottis marks a different region. Since the perturbation depends on the location within a mode, dropping the reference end can produce the wrong formant prediction.
rubric: Keep the endpoint attached to a fractional location.
Distinguish complementary descriptions from different physical regions.
Connect a location error with the subsequent mode analysis.
questions.topic: Reference points for a constriction location

questions.prompt: You want to determine whether the same proposed constriction region is motion-dominated in the first mode and deformation-dominated in the second. What should you compare in the animation?
questions.answer: I would keep the region fixed along the tract and inspect the first and second mode rows separately over their cycles. For each row I would compare particle excursion with local changes in neighbor spacing. The judgment concerns the same location in different spatial mode patterns, rather than comparing unrelated moments and treating a momentary zero displacement as a permanent node.
rubric: Hold the physical region fixed across the mode comparison.
Compare excursion and deformation across a cycle.
Avoid diagnosing the local role from one arbitrary phase alone.
questions.topic: Comparing modes at one physical region

questions.prompt: The source diagram associates a more tightly restoring, effectively lighter fold system with higher F0. Explain the cause-and-effect connection to the spacing of the spectral lines without calculating a rate.
questions.answer: A stronger restoring effect and less effective moving mass favor a faster back-and-forth fold cycle in the lecture’s mechanical comparison. A higher repetition rate gives more widely separated source harmonics. Inside the same frequency window, those wider intervals leave fewer components available to sample a vowel filter. The labels illustrate the mechanism rather than defining fixed anatomy for every speaker.
rubric: Connect restoring stiffness and moving mass with cycle speed.
Connect higher source repetition with wider harmonic spacing.
Explain the consequence within a shared frequency window.
questions.topic: Physical changes behind a wider source comb

questions.prompt: Using the filter examples on this page, explain why a recognizer receiving the first 300 Hz target alone could miss a distinction that an F1–F2 pair preserves.
questions.answer: The /u/ and /i/ or /I/ examples share that first target, so it does not distinguish the illustrated filters by itself. Their next targets differ, with /u/ showing 1000 Hz and /i/ or /I/ showing 2200 Hz. An ordered pair retains that additional relation, providing different input evidence even when the first coordinate matches.
rubric: Use the shared first target as an example of incomplete evidence.
Identify the differing next targets on this page.
Explain what an ordered feature pair adds.
questions.topic: Why one formant is insufficient for this comparison

questions.prompt: How would you use two comparisons in the source–filter grid to separate a changed vowel filter from changed source spacing?
questions.answer: First, compare panels across one source row to hold its F0 condition fixed while changing vowel columns. That reveals different filter shapes under a shared source. Then compare down one vowel column to hold its target resonances fixed while changing source rows. That reveals denser or sparser sampling of one filter. A diagonal comparison changes both factors and is harder to interpret.
rubric: Hold a source row fixed for the filter comparison.
Hold a vowel column fixed for the source comparison.
Explain why a diagonal change confounds the two factors.
questions.topic: Separating the two factors in a grid

questions.prompt: The /a/ filter illustration places targets close together at 800 and 900 Hz. Why is counting prominent colored harmonic stems in a dense or sparse source row an unreliable way to decide how many filter resonances are represented?
questions.answer: The two target resonances belong to the filter and are held fixed within that vowel column. Colored stems are available source harmonics shaped by the combined resonance envelope, so their number and prominence depend on the source spacing as well. Denser sampling can describe that envelope more fully, while sparse sampling can make the close targets hard to distinguish. Counting strong sampled lines does not directly count filter resonances, and dense sampling alone does not guarantee that two nearby resonances appear as two separate peaks.
rubric: Retain the two fixed filter targets in the column.
Distinguish available source components from underlying resonances.
Explain how sampling density affects the evidence without guaranteeing separate visible peaks.
questions.topic: Close formants and the limits of peak counting

questions.prompt: A filter makes one group of source harmonics prominent and attenuates another group. Why does that not by itself mean that the vocal folds have changed their repetition rate?
questions.answer: The filter changes relative amplitudes at the frequencies supplied by the source. F0 concerns the spacing of consecutive source components, not which group becomes strongest after filtering. A new envelope can therefore reflect a changed vocal-tract resonance pattern while the source repetition rate remains the same.
rubric: Explain filtering as relative amplitude shaping.
Use source component spacing rather than amplitude rank to distinguish F0.
Keep a changed envelope separate from a demonstrated source-rate change.
questions.topic: Filter selection without a new source pitch

questions.prompt: If you wanted the amplitude history of one fixed frequency, how would you read it from the spectrogram rather than follow a moving formant band?
questions.answer: I would retain the same vertical frequency position and move horizontally through time. The changing shade at that fixed height gives its amplitude under the supplied black–gray–white key. Following a curved formant band instead changes the frequency being sampled, so it answers a different question about the evolving resonance region.
rubric: Hold the frequency coordinate fixed.
Use horizontal time and the stated amplitude key.
Explain why tracking a moving band samples changing frequencies.
questions.topic: Reading one acoustic frequency through time

questions.prompt: Suppose one resonance band rises while retaining its shade, and another stays at the same height but darkens. Explain the two different observations under the illustrated key.
questions.answer: The first moves to a higher frequency without an indicated amplitude change under the stated conditions. The second gains amplitude at an unchanged frequency. Vertical position and darkness are separate encodings, so the two observations should not be collapsed into a single claim that both bands became higher pitched or louder.
rubric: Read the first change as a frequency shift.
Read the second as an amplitude change.
Preserve the unchanged quantity in each case.

questions.prompt: Why can sparse harmonic sampling matter to a recognizer that receives estimated F1 and F2, even before considering how its weights were learned?
questions.answer: The input features depend on identifying the filter’s resonances from the acoustic evidence. Sparse harmonics can make a resonance envelope ambiguous, making the feature estimate less securely supported. A network then receives those estimated values rather than direct access to the hidden filter. This concerns the evidence entering the classifier, not proof of a particular classification error or a change in its weights.
rubric: Connect the harmonic samples to the quality of resonance evidence.
Explain how estimated formants become classifier inputs.
Separate input uncertainty from a demonstrated model error.

questions.prompt: The hidden layers have three, two, and four units, while the outputs have five word labels. Why should hidden activations not simply be treated as extra measured formants or as words already recognized?
questions.answer: The measured formants enter as the two input values. Hidden units contain new numerical combinations formed by the network’s current connections, and their widths specify the intermediate representation sizes. The category names are attached to the five output units. The diagram does not give a separate physical resonance or a final word identity to each hidden unit.
rubric: Separate measured input features from computed hidden activations.
Explain hidden widths as representation sizes.
Retain word-category labels at the output stage.

questions.prompt: You want to test the effect of changing a fixed–fixed system to fixed–free. Why do two separately tuned examples with 100 Hz fundamentals not provide that controlled test, and what should you hold fixed?
questions.answer: Matching the displayed fundamentals does not establish that the two systems share the same length and wave speed. The source specifies that the examples were separately tuned. To isolate the boundary change, keep length and wave speed fixed while changing the endpoint condition. Under those ideal conditions, the fixed–free fundamental is half the fixed–fixed one. The equal 100 Hz labels therefore reflect the chosen comparison conditions rather than evidence that the boundary has no frequency effect.
rubric: Identify separate tuning as a changed comparison condition.
Hold length and wave speed fixed to isolate the boundary change.
State the qualitative halving prediction without treating matched labels as its measured result.

questions.prompt: Suppose the displayed random weights have been chosen and are then held fixed, with the same ordered input presented again. Why does the word “random” not by itself imply a new result on each forward pass?
questions.answer: Random describes how the weights were initially assigned. Once those parameters and the input are fixed, the declared sequence uses the same weighted linear operations again. No new random resampling step is specified for each pass. Different initialization and repeated inference through one fixed initialization are therefore different comparisons.
rubric: Distinguish a random initial assignment from repeated resampling.
Hold both the input and parameters fixed in the prediction.
Explain repeated use of the same specified operations.
questions.topic: Random initialization versus randomness on each pass

questions.prompt: Explain how a hidden neuron receiving positive formant inputs through both positive and negative connections can have contributions that partly oppose each other.
questions.answer: Each connection weights its own input. A positive input with a positive weight contributes positively, while a positive input with a negative weight contributes negatively. The neuron combines those terms, so one negative contribution does not determine the entire activation. This is signed internal arithmetic, distinct from interpreting a completed five-category probability distribution.
rubric: Explain the contribution signs without calculating products.
Describe the combination of opposing terms.
Separate internal signed values from output probabilities.

questions.prompt: Describe what must happen in a forward pass before a known answer could be used to improve the network, keeping computation and learning distinct.
questions.answer: The formant pair enters the first layer, and each layer forms activations from the preceding values and current weights until an output is obtained. A known answer could then be compared with that prediction to identify a mismatch. Using that information to change weights would be a separate learning step. Passing values through the network does not itself demonstrate that such a step has occurred.
rubric: Trace the ordered use of current weights through the layers.
Explain why a prediction is required before its mismatch can be assessed.
Distinguish computing activations from changing parameters.

questions.prompt: Suppose a teacher subsequently identifies a hypothetical example as /dean/, but the illustrated distribution favors /done/. Explain what the mismatch means without treating the display as an actual reported experiment.
questions.answer: The current prediction favors a different category from the supplied hypothetical target. The target identifies which output should receive stronger support, while the displayed probabilities describe the current preference. A learning procedure would try to change the weights to reduce that mismatch. The example illustrates the distinction between prediction and known label, not a measured accuracy result from this deck.
rubric: Separate the hypothetical target from the current preference.
Identify the disagreement at the category level.
Connect possible improvement to weight learning rather than relabeling the input.
questions.topic: Prediction versus a subsequently known label

questions.prompt: Explain why the declared sequence 2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5 is more than a list of independent layer sizes.
questions.answer: Each stage receives the preceding stage’s output. The three values produced by the first transformation are the three inputs of the next, its two values feed the two-input transformation after it, and the resulting four values feed the final four-input layer. The widths therefore describe connected interfaces, while the five final values correspond to the displayed category units.
rubric: Explain that one stage’s output is the next stage’s input.
Trace the matching widths through the declared order.
Connect the final width to the five category outputs.
questions.topic: Reading the code as connected interfaces

questions.prompt: The network contains several hidden layers. Why does that number of layers not contradict the slide’s description of this particular declaration as purely linear?
questions.answer: The displayed stages are linear transformations with bias removed, and no activation functions are inserted between them. Passing through several weighted linear stages does not add an omitted nonlinear operation. The claim concerns this stated model, rather than a claim that neural networks in general must use the same restricted architecture.
rubric: Use the actual linear-layer declarations and absence of activation functions.
Explain why additional stages do not supply a missing kind of operation.
Keep the conclusion limited to the declared architecture.
questions.topic: Why the declaration remains purely linear

questions.prompt: Before claiming that a trained formant recognizer identifies vowels accurately, what evidence would you want beyond a diagram showing information reaching five outputs?
questions.answer: I would want examples with measured formant pairs and independently known vowel identities, then compare the network’s decisions with those identities under stated conditions. The diagram establishes a proposed feature-to-category computation, while a numerical preference by itself does not establish correctness. The result should report what was actually evaluated rather than treat an intended training plan or schematic output as an observed success.
rubric: Specify input examples and independently known categories.
Compare predictions with those categories under stated conditions.
Distinguish a proposed computation from measured recognition performance.
questions.topic: Evidence for the proposed recognition task
